raw_text:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has undergone several dramatic paradigm shifts since its inception. While early balloon angioplasty was limited by acute vessel recoil and abrupt closure, the introduction of bare-metal stents (BMS) provided a rigid mechanical scaffold that successfully stabilized the vessel lumen [1]. However, BMS was plagued by high rates of in-stent restenosis due to neointimal hyperplasia, which was later resolved by drug-eluting stents (DES) [2]. Despite the unparalleled success of contemporary metallic DES, the lifelong presence of a permanent metallic "cage" prevents vascular restoration, limits natural vasomotion, hinders non-invasive imaging, and presents a perpetual substrate for late adverse events [2]. These challenges prompted the concept of transient vascular support—"leave nothing behind"—which initiated the development of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) [3].

The feasibility of using fully bioresorbable polymers for transient vascular support was first demonstrated using poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) backbones without drug elution, most notably the Igaki-Tamai scaffold [3]. Long-term evaluation over ten years validated the concept of complete scaffold resorption and late lumen enlargement, although these early devices lacked anti-proliferative drugs and had high clinical restenosis rates [4]. This paved the way for the first-generation everolimus-eluting PLLA-based Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular) [5]. Early feasibility studies demonstrated that the Absorb scaffold provided sufficient early radial strength and was completely resorbed within three years [6]. 

These promising findings led to the initiation of several landmark randomized controlled trials. Short-term (1-year) outcomes from the ABSORB II [7], ABSORB III [8], ABSORB Japan [9], and ABSORB China [10] trials demonstrated noninferiority of the BVS compared to state-of-the-art metallic cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (CoCr-EES). A large-scale, patient-level pooled meta-analysis at 1 year confirmed these findings, showing comparable safety and efficacy profiles between the BVS and CoCr-EES [11].

However, as patients were followed beyond the initial one-year mark, a troubling safety signal emerged. Long-term (3-to-5-year) results from ABSORB II [12], ABSORB III [13,14], and the AIDA trial [15] revealed a significantly higher risk of target lesion failure (TLF) and very late scaffold thrombosis (ScT) in the BVS cohort. Even in the large-scale, blinded ABSORB IV trial, which utilized optimized procedural strategies, BVS failed to demonstrate superiority in reducing angina and showed a persistent signal of increased late adverse events [16]. Meta-analyses of individual patient data confirmed that the risk of scaffold thrombosis peaked between one and three years post-implantation, leading to the clinical withdrawal of the first-generation Absorb BVS from the market [17,18].

In-depth investigations using intravascular imaging and histopathology clarified the underlying mechanisms of scaffold failure [19]. The primary mechanical vulnerabilities included underexpansion, severe late strut malapposition, and structural collapse during the resorption phase [19,20]. Furthermore, first-generation PLLA scaffolds had significantly thicker struts (~150 µm) compared to metallic DES (~80 µm) to maintain radial strength, which disrupted laminar blood flow, promoted platelet activation, and delayed endothelialization [21]. 

To mitigate these risks, experts advocated for the "PSP" technique: meticulous lesion **P**redilation, precise vessel **S**izing to avoid undersized scaffold deployment in small vessels, and high-pressure **P**ost-dilation [22]. Observational data validated that strict adherence to the PSP protocol significantly reduced scaffold thrombosis rates to levels comparable with metallic stents [22].

Rather than abandoning the concept, researchers focused on technological optimization [21]. This led to the development of bioresorbable metallic materials, predominantly magnesium alloys, which offer higher tensile strength and faster resorption times (typically 12 months) compared to PLLA [23]. The first-generation Drug-Eluting Absorbable Metal Scaffold (DREAMS-1) demonstrated safety and feasibility [23], leading to the development of the second-generation sirolimus-eluting magnesium scaffold (Magmaris, Biotronik) [24]. The BIOSOLVE-II trial [24] and subsequent BIOSOLVE registries [25,26] demonstrated excellent long-term clinical performance, low TLF rates, and a near-complete absence of scaffold thrombosis at five years [26]. Concurrently, alternative polymer designs were optimized. For instance, the iodinated desaminotyrosine polycarbonate-based Fantom scaffold offered thinner struts (125 µm) and improved radiopacity, yielding favorable clinical results in the FANTOM II trial [27,28].

More recently, the third-generation sirolimus-eluting resorbable magnesium scaffold (DREAMS 3G; Freesolve, Biotronik) has entered clinical evaluation [29]. Boasting refined mechanical properties, Freesolve features thinner struts (99–117 µm) and increased radial support while maintaining a fast resorption timeline [29]. The BIOMAG-I first-in-human study demonstrated that this third-generation device achieves optimal vascular healing, prevents late recoil, and successfully restores physiological vasomotor reactivity at one year [29,30].

While the first-generation BVS era was marked by early setbacks due to bulky strut profiles and suboptimal implantation techniques, it provided invaluable lessons on vascular mechanics and the absolute requirement for meticulous procedural optimization. Armed with thin-strut next-generation metallic and polymeric scaffolds, the "leave nothing behind" paradigm is experiencing a clinical renaissance, positioning bioresorbable vascular scaffolds as a highly refined option for customized coronary revascularization.
